profiles.meeting_scenario: A 30-minute brainstorming meeting in an academic ML systems lab between a faculty lead and a senior PhD student about a follow-up to NACHOS for submission to an efficient AI workshop. They are not locking implementation details yet; instead, they want 2-3 extension ideas that make hardware-constrained early-exit NAS look stronger for edge deployment while still being feasible within one semester. The agenda is to identify promising research angles, sketch how each would be framed experimentally, and decide what story to pitch at the next group meeting. The expected outcome is a shortlist of candidate directions with a seemingly shared narrative around latency-constrained search, admissible solutions, and joint design of backbone and exits.

members.name: Dr. Elena Varga
members.expertise: Neural architecture search, efficient deep learning, multi-objective optimization for edge AI
members.background: Elena leads a university ML systems group and has published on NAS, compression, and resource-aware model design, usually steering projects toward claims that are methodologically broad and experimentally defensible without requiring large engineering overhauls.
members.private_state: She wants a follow-up that looks clearly novel relative to NACHOS but can still reuse most of the current search code and training pipeline, so the team can produce strong preliminary results quickly.
hidden_assumptions: When people propose a 'latency-constrained' NAS extension, it is standard to mean latency estimated by a calibrated predictor or layerwise lookup table during search, with real-device timing used only for final validation.

An 'admissible' early-exit model respects the budget if its expected inference cost under the learned exit distribution stays below the target, because that is the natural quantity for Pareto selection in conditional computation.
A 'joint' search contribution means the backbone topology, exit placement, and auxiliary-head design are optimized together; confidence thresholds can be tuned afterward without weakening the claim.
For this project, 'the Jetson baseline' still refers to the lab's published Jetson Nano pipeline from the prior paper, because it is the benchmark already tied to the NACHOS codebase and figures.

If a student mentions deployment realism in brainstorming, that usually means improving the experimental story around the existing framework rather than putting device measurements directly inside the search loop.

members.name: Rohan Mehta
members.expertise: Early-exit networks, edge inference profiling, runtime-aware model evaluation
members.background: Rohan has been implementing and profiling conditional-compute models on Jetson and ARM devices, and he tends to reason from runtime behavior upward, especially around exit-path variability, calibration, and deployment tooling.
members.private_state: He wants the next project to hold up under systems-style scrutiny and feed directly into his thesis on deployable adaptive inference, even if that implies more engineering complexity than the lab usually prefers.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says 'latency-constrained' in 2026 for edge EENNs, they are implicitly committing to actual on-device timing for the relevant execution paths, not just a latency surrogate used during search.
An 'admissible' model should satisfy the deployment budget for each realized path or at least at a conservative percentile over inputs, because occasional late exits still break real-time guarantees.
A truly 'joint' design of an EENN includes the thresholding or gating behavior that determines when exits fire, since that policy materially changes the architecture's effective runtime signature.

Rohan presented his Orin Nano plus TensorRT profiling setup in the last internal group meeting, so he assumes it has become the new default meaning of 'the Jetson baseline' unless someone explicitly says 'Nano paper setup.'
If the project is pitched as deployment-oriented, then any hardware evaluation discussion naturally carries over to the same measurement setup he has already prepared for profiling.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss making the follow-up 'latency-constrained' or adding a stronger 'latency constraint' to the search.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means latency will be incorporated through an analytical surrogate during search, such as a lookup table or predictor fit from prior measurements, with hardware timings used only afterward to report final results.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means latency should be grounded in actual on-device timing of candidate behaviors or exit-path executions, because otherwise the constraint is not really about deployment latency.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are comfortable saying 'latency-constrained' without elaborating because in NAS discussions the phrase often suppresses the implementation detail of how latency enters the loop; at brainstorming stage, it sounds premature to specify the measurement mechanism.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of admissible under early exiting
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the method should return 'admissible models' under a compute or latency budget.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means admissibility is satisfied when the expected cost over the evaluation distribution, weighted by exit probabilities, remains under budget.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means admissibility should hold for each realized inference path or at least for a high-percentile path cost, so that rare expensive cases do not violate deployment constraints.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'admissible' comes from the prior NACHOS framing, so both inherit it as if its meaning were already settled; because both interpretations are technically reasonable for conditional computation, neither one feels like something that needs unpacking in a quick ideation meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to explore a more 'joint' design of the backbone and exits.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes backbone architecture, exit locations, and auxiliary-head structure inside the jointly searched object, while viewing threshold tuning as a post-search calibration step outside the core contribution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes threshold selection or gating policy as part of the jointly designed system, because the exit policy determines which computational paths are actually taken at inference time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'joint design' already sounds maximally inclusive, so both participants feel they have expressed a shared ambition; the omitted boundary around thresholding is a second-order scope assumption that rarely gets spelled out when brainstorming at a high level.

misalignment_points.topic: Which Jetson setup anchors the deployment story
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the Jetson baseline' or 'the Jetson results' as the obvious hardware anchor.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the lab's existing Jetson Nano benchmark from the prior NACHOS-style codebase, using the established PyTorch evaluation harness and preprocessing setup tied to their published figures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to his newer Jetson Orin Nano setup with TensorRT and fixed single-image inference, which he recently presented internally and now treats as the lab's standard deployment benchmark.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both setups are habitually shortened to 'the Jetson baseline' in lab conversation, and the ambiguity is reinforced by recency effects: M2 assumes his recent presentation updated the default, while M1 assumes the published benchmark remains the default for this project lineage.
